title: Whither Japan’s Three Non-Nuclear Principles?
author: TSURUOKA Michito
text:
The U.S. Navy ballistic missile submarine USS Pennsylvania (SSBN 735) travels through the Hood Canal as it returns home following a strategic deterrence patrol Oct. 16, 2014, in Puget Sound, Wash.
Credit: DoD photo by Chief Mass Communication Specialist Ahron Arendes, U.S. Navy/Released
Debate over the three non-nuclear principles has resurfaced in Japan as the government of Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae prepares a new National Security Strategy, due at the end of 2026. Even the status of the principles is contested. Some regard them as the country’s foundational principle (kokuze), while others describe them as a policy guideline, suggesting that the government is free to change it. Prime Minister Sato Eisaku first announced the principles in 1967, and the Diet has reaffirmed them on multiple occasions since then.The principles state that Japan will neither possess nor produce nuclear weapons, nor permit their introduction into its territory. As long as Japan remains a party to the Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), the only practical debate concerns the third principle: non-introduction. The commitments not to possess or produce nuclear weapons nevertheless sent an important message to the world when the principles were first articulated, before Japan ratified the NPT.[...]
